title: The CUDA Programming Model
blurb: Tests host and device code, threads, blocks and grids, the global index, grid-stride loops, the cost of moving data over PCIe, pinned memory and when not to over-use it, timing with CUDA events, and where the time went in a real vector-add pipeline.

refLinks.label: §39.2.3 Host <-> Device Memory: Two Worlds, One Bus
§39.2.4 Pinned Memory: Why the Transfer Speed Isn’t Fixed

questions.prompt: In a CUDA program, what does host code do?
options: Runs on the GPU and decides which kernel to run next by itself
Runs on the PCIe controller and schedules every memory transfer
Runs on every GPU thread at once and computes the result for one element each
Runs on the CPU, allocates GPU memory, copies data and launches kernels
questions.explanation: Host code is ordinary C++ on the CPU, and it is always in charge. Device code, the kernel, just computes on what the host handed it. The device never decides on its own what to do next.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter call the single most important practical lesson in learning CUDA?
options: How to write the fastest possible arithmetic in a kernel body
The cost of moving data between the two memory spaces
How to choose a block size that is a power of two
How to print from device code for debugging
questions.explanation: The chapter says understanding the host-device split, and the cost of transfers across it, matters more at first than anything about the kernel body. The worked example shows why.

questions.prompt: What can threads in the same block do that threads in different blocks can't?
options: Synchronise with __syncthreads() and share on-chip shared memory
Run on more than one SM at once, so they finish faster
Call other kernels directly, without going through the host or the driver
Read from global memory, which other blocks can't reach
questions.explanation: A block runs on one SM, so its threads can sync and share fast memory. Blocks run independently, in any order, possibly on different SMs, with no way to sync across them. All threads can read global memory.

questions.prompt: What is the most common way a thread computes its global index in a 1-D launch?
options: threadIdx.x * gridDim.x + blockIdx.x
gridDim.x * blockDim.x
blockIdx.x + threadIdx.x
blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x
questions.explanation: The block's index times the threads per block gives the block's starting offset, and threadIdx.x is the position inside it. gridDim.x * blockDim.x is the total thread count, which the grid-stride loop uses as its stride.

questions.prompt: In Listing 39.1's launch helloKernel<<<3, 4>>>(), what global thread id does block 2, thread 3 print?
questions.explanation: global_id = blockIdx.x × blockDim.x + threadIdx.x = 2 × 4 + 3 = 11. The launch makes 3 × 4 = 12 threads, with ids 0 to 11.

questions.prompt: Listing 39.1 calls cudaDeviceSynchronize() before returning. What happens without it?
options: The program may exit before the device prints anything.
The compiler rejects the file, since every kernel needs a sync.
The kernel runs twice, once per call to main and once at exit.
The output prints, but in reverse order of thread id.
questions.explanation: Launches are asynchronous, and device printf output is buffered until a sync. Without one, main() can return and the process exit first. The code compiles fine either way.

questions.prompt: What is the largest number of threads a single block can have?
options: 32, one warp
256, the usual block size
Unlimited, as long as the SM has registers to spare
questions.explanation: The chapter gives up to 1,024 threads per block. 32 is a warp, and 128 to 256 is a typical choice, not a limit.

questions.prompt: What does a grid-stride loop let a kernel do?
options: Handle any n with one fixed launch configuration
Skip elements that don't need processing, which saves memory
Synchronise threads across different blocks in the same launch
Run without any blocks, using only one large grid of threads
questions.explanation: Each thread processes element i, then i + stride, and so on, so a fixed grid covers any size. The launch configuration is tuned once per GPU, not per problem. It doesn't sync across blocks.

questions.prompt: Listing 39.2 launches grid = 1024 blocks of block = 256 threads. What is the loop's stride?
questions.explanation: stride = blockDim.x × gridDim.x = 256 × 1024 = 262,144, the total number of threads in the launch.

questions.prompt: With that stride of 262,144 and n = 1,000,000, how many elements does thread 0 process (indices 0, 262,144, and so on, while below n)?
questions.explanation: Thread 0 handles 0, 262,144, 524,288 and 786,432. The next, 1,048,576, is past n. That is 4 elements.

questions.prompt: Why must the block size be a multiple of 32?
options: The grid-stride loop only works when the stride is a power of two.
Shared memory is allocated in 32-byte units.
The warp is 32 threads, so other sizes leave part of a warp idle.
nvcc refuses to compile any other size.
questions.explanation: Threads execute in warps of 32. A block of 100 threads uses 4 warps, the last mostly empty. The chapter says block should be a multiple of 32, typically 128 to 256.

questions.prompt: Why is a copy from pageable host memory slower than one from pinned memory?
options: The driver must stage it through a temporary pinned buffer first, an extra copy.
The PCIe bus runs at half speed for any memory the OS might move.
Pageable memory sits on disk, so every copy waits for a disk read.
Pageable copies use the CPU, while pinned copies use the GPU's Tensor Cores to move data.
questions.explanation: The DMA engine needs a stable physical address. Pageable memory can move, so the driver copies it into a pinned staging buffer first. Pinned memory can be transferred directly.

refLinks.label: §39.2.4 Pinned Memory: Why the Transfer Speed Isn’t Fixed

questions.prompt: What does Listing 39.3 change to pin a host buffer?
options: A compiler flag, -pin, added to the nvcc command line
cudaMemcpy with an extra pinned argument on every call
cudaMalloc in place of new, which puts the buffer on the GPU
cudaMallocHost in place of new, and cudaFreeHost in place of delete[]
questions.explanation: Pinning is a one-line change in allocation, plus the matching free. cudaMalloc allocates GPU memory, which is a different thing.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter warn against pinning all of an application's host memory?
options: The GPU can only see 1 GB of pinned memory at a time.
Pinned memory is slower for the CPU to read, so all the CPU code would suffer.
Pinned memory can't be swapped, so over-pinning starves the OS of memory.
Pinned buffers are freed automatically after each kernel launch.
questions.explanation: Pin only buffers on frequent, performance-sensitive transfer paths. Locked pages are memory the rest of the system can't reclaim.

questions.prompt: Which practice does the chapter give for keeping transfers from dominating?
options: Copy data back to the host after every kernel, so no intermediate results are ever lost
Use smaller blocks, so each transfer moves fewer bytes at a time
Allocate all GPU memory with new, so the OS can manage it
Keep data on the GPU across many kernels, batch work, and overlap transfers with compute
questions.explanation: Real systems keep data resident, batch, and overlap copies with compute using CUDA streams. Copying back after every kernel makes transfers worse.

questions.prompt: In Listing 39.4, why is cudaEventSynchronize(stop) called before cudaEventElapsedTime?
options: To make the kernel run on every SM at once
To wait until the stop event has completed, so the elapsed time is real
To reset both events to zero before the next measurement
To copy the kernel's output back to the host first
questions.explanation: The kernel and the stop record are queued asynchronously. Waiting on the stop event ensures the timed work is finished before the time is read.

questions.prompt: In the pageable run (H2D 19.2 ms, kernel 0.53 ms, D2H 54.5 ms), what took most of the time?
options: Moving data across PCIe
Allocating memory on the GPU
Compiling the kernel with nvcc
The vector-add kernel itself
questions.explanation: About 74 ms of the 74.2 ms total was transfers. The kernel was under 1% of it. That is the chapter's central surprise.

questions.prompt: Pinning cut D2H from 54.469 ms to 9.263 ms. By what factor? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: 54.469 / 9.263 = 5.88, about 5.9x, from one changed allocation line.

questions.prompt: In the pinned run, the kernel took 0.463 ms of a 28.287 ms total. What percentage is that? Give one decimal place.
questions.explanation: 0.463 / 28.287 = 0.0164, or 1.6%. Even after the transfer fix, the kernel stayed a tiny share of the pipeline.

questions.prompt: A teammate wants to spend a week optimising this vector-add kernel's arithmetic. What does the chapter's result suggest?
options: Go ahead, since pinned memory already fixed the transfers completely.
Check where time goes first. The kernel was about 2% of the total, so its arithmetic barely matters here.
Go ahead, since the kernel is the only part of the pipeline that runs on the GPU.
Rewrite it in Triton, since CUDA C++ kernels are always transfer-bound.
questions.explanation: The chapter's lesson: before optimising arithmetic, check where the time goes. Even perfect kernel code would save at most about 2% here. Transfers, still 98% after pinning, are where the time is.

bookExercises.prompt: In your own words, explain the difference between a block and a grid, and state which of the two can synchronise internally with `__syncthreads()`.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A block is a group of up to 1024 threads that run together on a single SM. Blocks are the unit that can synchronise internally, using `__syncthreads()`, and can share fast on-chip shared memory. A grid is the full collection of blocks launched by one kernel call. Blocks within a grid run independently, potentially on different SMs and in any order, with no mechanism to synchronise across blocks.

bookExercises.prompt: Write the one-line global thread ID formula this chapter calls "arguably the single most important line of code in CUDA," and explain what each of its four terms refers to.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `int global_id = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;`. `blockIdx.x` is the calling thread's block index within the grid, `blockDim.x` is the number of threads per block, and `threadIdx.x` is the calling thread's index within its own block. Multiplying the block index by the block size and adding the thread's local index gives a single flat index unique across the whole grid.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 39.2 as a starting point, explain what would happen, correctness-wise, not just performance-wise, if `grid * block` were smaller than `n` and the `stride` loop were removed (i.e., each thread processed only a single element via `if (i < n)` instead of `while`).
bookExercises.modelAnswer: If `grid * block < n` and the stride loop is replaced with a single `if (i < n)` check, every thread would compute at most one element, and any element with a flat index `i >= grid * block` would never be written by any thread at all. The output array would be left partially uninitialised (whatever garbage was in device memory beforehand) for all the "extra" elements beyond the launched thread count. This is a correctness bug, not just a performance regression. The grid-stride `while`/`for` loop is what guarantees every element gets processed regardless of how the launch configuration compares to `n`.

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter measured a pageable D2H transfer of 54.469 ms and a pinned D2H transfer of 9.263 ms for a 134.2 MB array. Compute the effective bandwidth in GB/s for each case, and compare both against Chapter 38's roughly 1.7 TB/s peak bandwidth estimate for this book's reference rig.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Bytes moved for one 134.2 MB array: `n * 4 bytes = 33,554,432 * 4 = 134,217,728 bytes ≈ 0.1342 GB`. Pageable D2H: `0.1342 GB / (54.469 / 1000) s ≈ 2.46 GB/s`. Pinned D2H: `0.1342 GB / (9.263 / 1000) s ≈ 14.49 GB/s`. Both figures are one to three orders of magnitude below Chapter 38's roughly 1.7 TB/s on-GPU memory bandwidth estimate. That's expected, since PCIe host↔device transfer is a completely different interconnect from on-die HBM bandwidth, and pageable transfers pay an additional staging-copy tax on top of the PCIe link's own ceiling. That's exactly why the pinned number is nearly 6x higher than the pageable one despite moving the identical bytes over the identical physical link.

bookExercises.prompt: The Worked Example found the kernel was under 1% of total pipeline time. Using Listing 39.4, describe how you would confirm this same imbalance exists (or doesn't) for a kernel that does substantially more arithmetic per element than a vector add.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Wrap the compute-heavy kernel launch with Listing 39.4 exactly as the H2D/kernel/D2H stages were each individually timed in the Worked Example, then compare the kernel's elapsed time against the H2D and D2H stage times measured for the same problem size. If the kernel does substantially more arithmetic per element (e.g. a small loop of transcendental functions per element rather than one add), its share of total pipeline time should grow relative to the roughly 1% seen for vector-add. The point is to actually re-measure per-stage rather than assume the same imbalance holds for a different kernel body.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague proposes pinning every host buffer in a large training pipeline "to be safe." Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, write the two or three sentences you'd say back.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Pinning every host buffer removes the "which buffers actually matter" decision, but it isn't free. Pinned memory can't be swapped to disk, so pinning a large fraction of a training pipeline's host memory starves the OS and other processes of memory they need, and can even fail outright under memory pressure. The right approach is to pin only the buffers that sit on a frequent, performance-sensitive transfer path, exactly the ones this chapter's D2H measurement showed benefiting, not every host allocation in the program.

bookExercises.prompt: Design a scenario (in one or two sentences, no code required) where Unified Memory (`cudaMallocManaged`) would be a reasonable choice over the explicit `cudaMalloc`/`cudaMemcpy` pattern this chapter teaches, and one where it would clearly be the wrong choice.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Unified Memory is reasonable for a fast prototype or research script that moves data between host and device only occasionally and where development speed matters more than shaving milliseconds off transfers, e.g., quickly testing whether an algorithm produces correct results at all. It is clearly the wrong choice for a latency-sensitive production pipeline with frequent, large, predictable transfers on a hot path, exactly this chapter's vector-add pipeline, where explicit `cudaMalloc`/`cudaMemcpy`, plus pinned memory, gives the control and predictability needed to hit a measured performance target.

bookExercises.prompt: Skim the "Data Transfer" chapter of the NVIDIA CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide. Summarise, in a few sentences, what CUDA streams add on top of the pinned-memory optimisation in this chapter, and why streams require pinned memory to be effective.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, no single answer expected. CUDA streams let independent chunks of work (transfers and kernel launches) be queued so that a H2D transfer for one chunk of data can overlap with kernel execution on a previously-transferred chunk, and with a D2H transfer of an even earlier chunk's results. This turns what this chapter measured as three strictly sequential stages into a pipeline where the GPU's copy engines and compute units are busy simultaneously. Streams require pinned memory specifically because the DMA engine driving an asynchronous, overlapped transfer needs a stable physical address for the whole transfer's duration. A pageable buffer could be relocated by the OS mid-transfer, which is exactly why pageable copies are forced through a synchronous staging copy in the first place, and why that staging behavior is incompatible with genuine overlap.
